body:
_Migrated from issue #1104, filed 2026-07-25._

Split out of #1103, where shipping a fix inline would have changed behaviour for existing users without warning.

## The bug

`cps/web.py` routes `GET /robots.txt` at `send_from_directory(constants.STATIC_DIR, "robots.txt")`. That file has never existed — not in this repo's history, and not in `janeczku/calibre-web`, which the route is inherited from. So the route is a guaranteed 404 in every deployment, on this build and on stock Calibre-Web.

Confirmed live on `cwn-local`:

```
$ curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://localhost:8086/robots.txt
404
```

A crawler that gets no answer there applies its own default and crawls whatever it can reach. On a server with anonymous browsing enabled that means the catalogue — and by extension what the people using the server read — can end up in search results.

## Why it isn't a one-line fix

Dropping in a `Disallow: /` default de-indexes every already-public instance on upgrade. That's a real regression for a group we know exists: `cps/admin.py:166` reads `GOOGLE_SITE_VERIFICATION` from the environment and nine templates emit `<meta name="google-site-verification">`, so the app already ships first-class support for operators who register their instance with Google Search Console. Those operators deliberately want indexing.

The deeper problem is that the route promises something a user has no supported way to provide: `cps/static/` is baked into the image, so in Docker there's no way to supply a `robots.txt` short of bind-mounting over a path inside the application tree.

## Options

1. **Admin setting** — a crawl-policy field (block all / allow all / custom body) rendered by the route. Most discoverable, matches how the rest of the app is configured, and makes the default an explicit choice rather than a silent one.
2. **Derive from `config_anonbrowse`** — no UI, but it guesses at operator intent, and "I enabled anonymous browsing for my family's LAN" and "I run a public library" are not the same thing.
3. **Ship a permissive default** (`User-agent: * / Disallow:`) — fixes the 404 with zero behaviour change, but is semantically identical to the 404 for a compliant crawler, so it fixes nothing a user would notice.
4. **Delete the dead route.**

Option 1 looks right: it fixes the 404, makes the policy explicit, gives Docker users a supported way to set it, and preserves current behaviour for anyone who doesn't touch it. Whatever lands should also be verified over HTTP against a live container, not just as a file-exists assertion.
title: GET /robots.txt returns 404 in every deployment — needs a crawl-policy decision
